utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just make the point that we are now in open session, so your Honour is quite aware of that. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I am aware of this. Now following the decision of the Trial Chamber, we referred the complaint to the President for investigation. In making our reference we requested that the investigation should go into the circumstances of the leakage of the information of the list of witnesses; secondly, to make a determination as to the responsibility otherwise of any one counsel appearing in the Celebici proceedings and to other persons connected with the custody of the witness lists; three, we also requested there should be a determination of the fact of the leakage upon the current proceedings. I hear the report has been circulated to all counsel, and the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: So you all have copies. Now instead of going into the lengths of the report, I think the important part is just paragraph 7, which concludes -- and the conclusions of the President are stated in paragraph 7(a) and (b). Paragraph (a) clearly stated that: "There is no evidence of misconduct -- with regard to Defence Counsel Edina Residovic and Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan there is no evidence of misconduct on their part. (b) With regard to the Defendant Zejnil Delalic, it would seem likely that the Defendant Zejnil Delalic gave a telephone interview to the magazine Sloboda Hercegovina. This interview was published in the 15 April 1997 issue of the said magazine. It would seem that in the course of interview the Defendant Zenjil Delalic mentioned the name of at least one witness which appears on the Prosecutor's witness list that is the subject of the Order for Non-Disclosure. It would therefore appear that the Defendant Zejnil Delalic might have acted in contempt of the Order for Non-Disclosure. In this regard the Prosecutor may want to consider whether it is appropriate to initiate proceedings against Mr. Delalic for contempt of the Tribunal pursuant to Rule 77(C) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. (c) With regard to the author of the articles in question, Mr. Tahir Pervan, and the editor of the newspaper in question, regretfully investigations have been inconclusive". This is the conclusion of the President. As far as the Trial Chamber is concerned, since all participating in the judicial process here have been cleared of any wrongdoing, I think we are comfortable in carrying on as we have always done. As I said at the beginning and I think this has been confirmed by the investigation, we have always had the highest regard for the integrity, professional competence and dedication of counsel in this case in doing all they can in bringing justice before this Trial Chamber. We have been justified in this conviction. I think this is all the Trial Chamber has to say on this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: May I address the court? I appear for Mr. Delalic on this particular issue of contempt in the President's report. You will see my name mentioned there. I was brought in to deal with this particular matter because of the conflict that there was between this matter and his lawyers on the main indictment. As you have stated in the opening remarks, the object of the exercise was to seek a determination of the issues and I, with respect, echo your Honour's observations as to the finding in respect of the lawyers involved. That may be regarded as a determination, although it is not for me to say so, but it is plain there has been no determination of the issue in respect of Mr. Delalic. A determination of an issue means the issue has been decided one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak up a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Determination --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please switch on your microphone. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You can leave it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Is it working now. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Take your finger out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I am grateful for that assistance. A determination presupposes that an issue has been decided. In this case the issue, the central issue, is whether or not there had been a material contempt of this court in respect of the publication of information or names that should not have been published under the rules of the court. We are left in this position, with respect, that Mr. Delalic is in exactly the same position that he was in when the issue was first raised some week ago. It is still not clear whether or not he faces an issue for contempt or indeed how that issue of contempt may be resolved. It can, with respect, only be resolved by the accumulation of evidence which is accumulated and presented within the rules of the Tribunal. That is that witnesses would be seen, they would be interviewed under caution, and either by oral or videotape that evidence would be presented to the defence and they would be able to conduct their own investigation in exactly the same way as any other matter that came before the Tribunal. Now, that position has simply not yet been reached. What the Honourable President has done is effectively invited the prosecution to consider whether or not they intend to proceed along that path, and if I may, with respect, quote from paragraph 7B, what the learned President has done is to draw sort of suppositions from the material which is available, the newspaper articles, which one could have drawn a week ago and, of course, he had no option but to do that, because there is, in fact, no evidence beyond those articles. That is demonstrated clearly, with respect, by the use of these words. Paragraph 7(b): "With regard to the Defendant Zejnil Delalic, it would seem likely that he gave a telephone interview". I turn over the page. The first words of the first sentence on page 4: "It would seem that in the course of the interview ..." I go on four lines down: "It would therefore appear that ..." On the same line: "... might have acted in contempt of the Order for Non-Disclosure. It goes on to say: "The Prosecutor may want to consider ..." All that may mitigate against there having been any determination of this matter in any manner, shape or form. The matter is still very much at large. In my respectful submission, your Honour, the problem is this, that if there is an attempt to go forward in this case without having first resolved, determined the issue of contempt, which was the object of the exercise a week ago, any evidence which is now called in respect of this matter by the prosecution is going to be tainted by the suspicion, because suspicion it remains, that Mr. Delalic has had something to do with a fundamental concept, which may go to the very heart of that evidence. This is not a peripheral contempt of court that is being alleged. Sometimes there is a contempt of court where a witness makes an outburst, where somebody in the public gallery does something. That is a relatively minor and peripheral contempt that can be dealt with on a summary basis and is often done so, but this is a fundamental allegation of a contempt which goes to the very heart of the case and to the probity of any evidence which is called. That is as to the Prosecution evidence. It is even worse, in my submission when we come to consider the evidence that the defendant may give on his own behalf or may call on his behalf or indeed that other defendants may give or may call, although that is a matter of consideration by their counsel, because all of that evidence is going to be tainted with the suspicion until the matter is determined one way or the other that that evidence is coloured by a consideration of contempt for this Tribunal. Now, in those circumstances it is my submission that it would be impossible for this or, indeed, any Tribunal to consider that evidence in the absence of the prejudice that would arise by virtue of that contempt. We know it is a fundamental principle of the rule of justice that justice must not only be done but it must manifestly be seen to be done. May I draw an analogy? If there was a trial by jury where the Tribunal was concerning just issues of law and the jury were concerning issues of fact, the question of any contempt, as indeed the existence of any other indictment, would be withheld from the jury. The reason it would be withheld from the jury is the reason that I have just submitted, because of the devastating effect it would have upon their consideration of the evidence. In this Tribunal, as a matter of fact and procedure, of course the Tribunal sits on both questions of fact and law, but where that is the case, then everything must be done that is practicable to be done to make the proceedings as fair and just as possible for the defendants and the co-defendants, so that any suspicion that the Tribunal might have had other matters in their mind at the time they were concerning the central issues on the indictment can safely be put to one side. It is practicable in this case to achieve that position. In my submission, it is practicable in this way. The Honourable President has invited the prosecution to consider their position and to determine whether or not they wish to pursue contempt proceedings against Mr. Delalic. They now have the opportunity to do that in a way where they can gather evidence that would fall within the Rules of Procedure of this Tribunal. People can be interviewed under caution and on tape and the weight of that evidence can be determined, because at the moment it is mere supposition, and they will need to gather evidence to be in a position to be able to say properly to themselves and properly to this Tribunal: "We have evidence that we consider is proper, probative evidence that goes to this contempt and therefore it would be proper to try this man." As a rough rule of thumb, and I can only speak for my own jurisdiction, the Crown Prosecution Service in the United Kingdom only prosecute a case whereupon consideration of the evidence there is at least a 50 per cent chance of a conviction. It would seem, with the greatest respect, in my submission, there is nothing wrong with that approach for the prosecution in this case. They cannot do that until they have got evidence as opposed to material from only which supposition can be drawn. They are, therefore, now in a position to devise a procedure to have an independent investigator, who would have all the powers of investigation within the rules of the Tribunal, to accumulate that evidence and to bring it before this Tribunal. I say it, and I say it with the greatest respect, it is perhaps a good thing that, in fact, the Honourable President did not manage to accumulate anything which would be properly regarded as evidence, because when one thinks about it, he would have been in this invidious position, that had he done so he might have been in a position where he would have to be called as a witness before this Tribunal, which would have been a difficult state of affairs. It is so much better if there is an independent investigator appointed by the Prosecutor who can become a witness in the case and perhaps almost inevitably would become a witness in the case and can give evidence before this Tribunal without the difficulties and embarrassment it would have caused had the Honourable President been put into that difficult position. What I say in my closing submission is this: it is impossible in this case for the defendant Mr. Delalic to have this case continue against him and feel that the Tribunal is able to distinguish between the suspicion that falls against him and remains against him until the matter is determined and have the matters contained on indictment considered in isolation, the necessary isolation to give those matters the proper weight and consideration to which he is entitled, and to which as a matter of practicalities the prosecution is also entitled, because if he is not, one can see how that could well in the fullness of time give rise to an expensive and time-consuming appellate hearing. With the greatest respect, my submissions are designed not to create but to avoid delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHITE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Morrison. I appreciate your position and your apprehension about the subsequent course of events. I suppose in this regard -- I think the trump card lies with the prosecution, because they have merely called upon to consider whether there is sufficient evidence to proceed against him. They need not proceed unless they are convinced that it is worth proceeding and there is sufficient evidence for them to do so. It is only on that basis that the prosecution would take up the invitation for them to do so by the President. I think we might hear them when they might have considered the matter. To see what cause of action they tend to adopt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: The position in my submission is plain. The prosecution have been invited and they must make up their mind how to proceed. It is not, with the greatest of respect, a burden upon the Tribunal. It is a burden upon the prosecution, but the fundamental problem remains, and I would invite them to do as speedily as is practical, that evidence before -- I appreciate in the English Bar the prosecutors can defend and I probably prosecute more than I defend so I do appreciate the difficulties they have, but the reality of that position is they cannot make that decision until they are in posession of the evidence. It seems to be, looking at the report of the honourable president, that the evidence really falls into a very narrow orbit. He has concentrated on and there is a named individual -- I will not name him; he is the journalist named in paragraph 6 and his editor -- it seems to me with a certain amount of diligence and enthusiasm the question of any evidence from that source can be investigated really within a matter of a day or two. The Honourable President managed to track this man down and would have been in a position, had he been interested in giving evidence, to take evidence from him. The prosecution are perhaps in a better position than the Honourable President was, because they can appoint a Prosecutor, and that can be done really in a matter -- an investigator rather. That can be done as a matter of urgency. This matter could be resolved in a matter of days if the conclusion is that the prosecution are not going to proceed with any allegation of contempt, and the Tribunal can then get back to its main task of considering the indictment. If the prosecution, however, on considering the evidence come to the conclusion that there is a prosecutable offence, then plainly the question of whether or not that should be done before, as I have submitted it should be, the continuation of the trial remains a live issue. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. Ms. Residovic? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, please allow me to present two issues related to the consideration of the report submitted by Mr. President. First of all, I would like to thank both the Trial Chamber and the President for trying to resolve very serious issues in such a short time, the issues that came before this Trial Chamber. I have been able to go through the report, in particular through the paragraph 7, and please allow me, therefore, to say two things. The President in paragraph 7 submitted his personal conclusion related to the facts he has been able to establish in the course of his investigation. I am glad and I appreciate the position taken by this Trial Chamber when it comes to the defence of Mr. Delalic, defence counsel, and their attempts to continue to provide a fair and just defence for their clients. However, your Honours, I think that even as regards this issue we did not go much further than at the last hearing before this Chamber. The personal conclusion of the President contained in his report on the investigations conducted, as far as I am familiar with the rules of this Tribunal, is not a basis on which the defence counsel could be absolutely excluded from any further proceedings which are in the sole domain of the Prosecutor. I would like to remind you, your Honours, that the discussion on this issue began with the question made by the Prosecutor and his statement -- their statement before this Trial Chamber. I refer to the French transcript, page 1731, lines 31, where it was stated before this Trial Chamber that: "This case in all probability, as it appeared at that time that, one of the defence counsel and one of the defendants was involved in this case". So when this first situation is in question, the way that the defence counsel should be treated has not been resolved in this report by the President. It should be resolved by the Prosecutor and the Prosecutor should make their position clear. As regards any future or existing facts that may come up in the investigations conducted by the prosecution, we do not have any position from them on that, and therefore it is my view that the position of the defence counsel in this case has not changed, let alone the position of our client. I, therefore, think that even this paragraph without the clear position made by the prosecution cannot be completely unequivocal before this Trial Chamber, and therefore our view in the continuation of this proceeding as regards any future possible conflict of interests between us and the client will also remain unchanged as to what I said last time. The second issue is the question of our client. Your Honours, both myself and Professor O'Sullivan are here in this court room only to represent and to defend the interests of our client. We do not wish to put him in a position which may either in this proceeding or in some other proceedings endanger his interests. So if the issue of the position of his defence counsel is solved once and for all decisively, then we as his defence counsel in this proceeding will honour the position of our learned colleague, Mr. Morrison, whether the continuation of this proceeding could prejudice his interest as to any other proceedings. Therefore, I would like to ask this Trial Chamber to request that the prosecution solve the entirety of this problem because I think we cannot have a fair trial of my client without this. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you, Ms. Residovic. Tom Moran, do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Tom Moran for Hazim Delic. Judge, initially I want to make it very clear that I do not have a dog in the fight with Mr. Delalic, but I would like to introduce for the purposes of this only a decision signed by the Registrar on the 23rd, and which was delivered to me today. My big worry is prejudice to my client. I move to introduce this as Delic exhibit next just for the purposes of this proceeding. I have not thought through what I think needs to be done, because I just got this an hour and a half ago, but I am worried the fall-out could hurt my client. The Registrar has found that there is reasonable grounds for believing that my client, Mr. Landzo and Mr. Mucic may attempt to interfere or intimidate witnesses or otherwise disturb the maintenance and good order of the detention unit. I believe this is growing out of the same type of allegations. Now, I have heard no evidence from anyone that my client is involved in this, yet I find a distinguished former judge, the Registrar of this court, of the Tribunal, making this kind of finding. The fact that my client's phone calls are going to be monitored do not bother me one way or the other. I do not particularly care. What I am worried about is there is this broad brush painting of people when there is no evidence at all that I have heard, no reasonable grounds that my client did anything. I would like to see this issue put to bed so that Hazim Delic does not get hurt by the fall-out. Thank you very much, judge. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much, Mr. Moran. This is an administrative decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think the channel of complaint is to the President, not directly to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I concede that. I am not asking the Trial Chamber to do anything about this. I am just pointing out that if the Registrar, who is a person that I admire very much, makes this kind of finding, I am worried that perhaps in all good faith in this courtroom some of this fall-out may hit my client. It makes me again very nervous. I would like this thing put to bed and somebody to stand up there and say "Hazim Delic may have done a lot of things in his life, but this is not one of them". JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Can we hear the Prosecutor as to what he thinks?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Just to the point raised by Mr. Moran, this is an administrative thing which we dealt with in the 64 hearing this morning, and I think that is nothing -- as your Honour just said, nothing for the Trial Chamber to worry about. To the main issue, I just, as all of us, got this report from the President and I read 7A with regard to the defence counsel Edina Residovic and Eugene O'Sullivan there is no evidence of misconduct on their part and I have nothing to add at all to that. I would just say that that made me -- should make me stand up and say: "We are ready to proceed." Speaking for the civil law system where I come from, the question of contempt of court would be dealt with totally separately and should not be considered in the way now raised before this Tribunal. In my view this could also from our point of view be handled separately without -- I have the absolute conviction that the Trial Chamber can separate the one thing from the other, and that it should not be tolerated to taint anything at all during the proceedings. I cannot now, just having read this, say exactly what is the Prosecutor going to do about the invitation from the President. Something might or might not be done, but I cannot stand up here today and say: "We are not going to do anything at all or Prosecutor is going to do this in that way at that time or what time." I know nothing about that. My position is that this is a separate matter that should not delay these proceedings. I would ask your Honour to invite Ms.. McHenry to have some points of view from the common law points of view maybe. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Very briefly, your Honour, the matter was referred to the President and he has given us a report in which he states that there is no evidence suggesting that defence counsel was involved. The prosecution has never suggested that defence counsel was involved, and I believe that -- I do not know if there is a mistranslation, but at least the English transcript makes clear that the prosecution has not suggested that defence counsel was involved. As I believe Mr. Ostberg has said on several occasions, we do not have evidence and we are not suggesting that defence counsel is involved. We believe that we can, with both the finding of the President and the current state, we can proceed and that there is not a conflict of interest. The matter has been referred to the prosecution for consideration. As Mr. Ostberg has said, the prosecution will consider what to do about it, but that does not impact on the ability of these proceedings to go forward. I believe even the suggestion that has been raised, and this is really an issue for Mr. Delalic and Ms. Residovic with respect to the pending proceedings that are on-going, that somehow even the suggestion might taint the Trial Chamber, and we have no -- the prosecution has no doubt whatsoever that your Honours will be able to hear the pending proceedings, which is the indictment against Mr. Delalic and the others, based upon the evidence that is brought before you here in court, and that you will not be tainted in any way whatsoever by any suppositions or things outside what is brought here as evidence. Your Honours do this every day. The situation is no different than if there was another indictment against Mr. Delalic which was separate from the current case. Certainly your Honours would be able to hear one case without considering the fact that there is an indictment or whatever. Here we have even less. There is no charge against Mr. Delalic for anything. There is absolutely no reason why this case, the indictment against Mr. Delalic and the other accused cannot go forward now. What, if anything, the prosecution chooses to do separately with the contempt does not now have any impact on these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was a matter which really related to the submission I made. May I just answer it briefly? With great respect to my learned friend, she is misdirecting her mind as to the issue. The question of whether or not Mr. Delalic faced a separate indictment is easily distinguishable on this basis. If he faced a separate indictment that this Trial Chamber knew about, it would be a separate indictment that involved quite separate issues of evidence. If it did not involve separate issues of evidence it would hardly be a separate indictment. The problem in this case is that the contempt relates to the evidence before the tribunal on this indictment, the indictment that they are hearing, and that is the fundamental difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There seems to be some kind of problem in the interpretation booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are having problems with the volume. Could you please speak up a little bit. We are asking the technicians to increase the volume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I am sorry. It is just my lack of desire to shout, but I will do better. The issue is fundamentally different. It is not just different in issue; it is different in kind. This is an issue which goes to the heart of the evidence on this indictment. To suggest that there is an analogy between a case where there is another indictment concerning completely different evidence is, with great respect, misguided. The question of the strength and indeed the expansion of my submission is only one that can be made in reality before this Tribunal once the Prosecution have acceded to the learned President's invitation and made up their mind whether they are going to go ahead and prosecute Mr. Delalic for contempt. If they choose not to do so, all well and good. If they choose to do so, then the question of whether or not that hearing should take place before, during or after the main indictment is a separate issue to be determined at that stage, but what has to be determined first is the issue of whether or not the prosecution in this case are going to pursue a charge or indictment against Mr. Delalic. Secondly, a minor point, the question of conflict of interests between a lawyer and client, that is between Mr. Delalic and his other lawyers in this case, is a matter for them and for Mr. Delalic. It is not, with the greatest respect, a matter for the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to add one quick thing. Mr. Ostberg said that my complaint was settled in a Rule 64 hearing this morning. I know there was a Rule 64 hearing this morning. I was not a party to it, was not invited to it. In fact, it was in closed session. If my client was dealt with in a hearing which we had no notice of and, in fact, were not each allowed to hear, I would be very surprised. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Mr. Ostberg, let me find out. You have been invited by the President to consider the question of contempt of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Now are you making up your mind outside the findings of the President or within the findings which we are relying upon?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I cannot rule out that that would be considered with finding outside what the President has found in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I wonder whether I might just take a moment of your Honour's time? Can I explain what I think may be the difficulty in this case? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let us suppose for a moment that the trial continues on the main indictment and the prosecution are carrying out a parallel investigation and indict Mr. Delalic with an offence of contempt and that matter remains unresolved. During the course of the trial a witness for the prosecution shows all the signs of having become a hostile witness and for whatever reason it then becomes a matter of suspicion as to why that witness has become hostile. In that manner I hope I demonstrate the possibility that there is a potential connection between a parallel investigation as yet unresolved into a question of contempt and to the issue of why a witness has become hostile. Your Honours have to sit here and assess each witness as they come to give evidence and as they give evidence determine whether they are witnesses who are both honest and accurate. If at the back of everybody's mind is the issue of whether or not Mr. Delalic has committed a contempt by attempting to intimidate witnesses and there is any suspicion that a witness has become hostile because of that activity, there is the clear relationship between the on-going, unresolved inquiry into contempt and the trial. It would be an injustice if at the end of the case Mr. Delalic was cleared of the contempt but for a time consideration of witnesses had been conducted by your Honours against the background of that on-going suspicion. So your Honours, in my submission, have to look at each witness knowing what the position as far as Mr. Delalic is concerned is, so that you can assess have they been interfered with. Is that the reason why they are giving evidence in this way? Until the conclusion has been reached one way or the other, and I enter not into the Prosecution's decision in any way, but until that matter is resolved, your Honours, with respect, and I mean this with respect, cannot be seen by the outside world -- it comes back to my learned friend Mr. Morrison's phrase about justice not only being done but manifestly being seen to be done -- if there is any suspicion that there is any interference with a witness and that consideration has been coloured by the accusation or the suspicion, then there is a danger that the consideration -- the defendant's interests are being damaged in some way. That is the concern I think that may exist. That is where the relationship lies between the inquiry into contempt, which is a fundamental one, and this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Please read Rule 77C.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am going to have to ask one of my learned friends to lend me a copy because I have left mine in the robing room, for which I apologise for being adequately equipped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is probably the one you have in mind. 77C.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: My learned friend Mr. Morrison has kindly lent me his. That is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That would have to be a separate enquiry altogether, namely disclosure of names of the witnesses will not be tantamount to interfering or intimidating a witness. Why do you suppose if a witness turns hostile the assumption would be that he has been interfered with or intimidated?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: One has to go back to the basics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Every time a witness turns hostile we would be holding an inquiry?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No, I am not suggesting that. What I am suggesting is let us suppose it is one of those, for example, to whom protection measures relate. Why are there protection measures in existence in relation to a particular witness? It is in order to prevent them from becoming intimidated. If they unexpectedly turn hostile and theirs was one of the names that was named in the list, there is the relationship, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is a big jump.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I do not think it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Interfere with, some positive act.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Interfere with is a positive act. Intimidation is a positive act.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course, but one then looks at the idea of, if you will bear this in -- let us assume for the moment that the act was done by the defendant. What would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is a big jump.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, but what would be the purpose of publishing these things other than to do that, if that is what he did and I do not for the moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is no evidence for the moment that he did and the President has left the question entirely open. Maybe the prosecution decides not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe the prosecution decides not to proceed further. Why should we hold up the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Absolutely, but what I am trying to demonstrate is that there is the potential which can arise. Again it is the crystal ball thing. We cannot see a week down the line where someone turns up to court, gives evidence and immediately gives signs of having been interfered with by somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That will then be a separate inquiry altogether, not connected with this inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course, but at the back of the defendant's mind, as he sees your Honour considering the witnesses, what is he thinking? He may be thinking: "Gosh! They think I have done this".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is why he has legal counsel available to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that. All I am trying to demonstrate is there is a potential relationship between the on-going inquiry and what might happen here. It is not, I think, a fanciful one. It is one that is potentially realistic. That is the relationship and the concern that he may have. I do not know. I may be entirely wrong about that, but I can well see that that might happen and be thought to cause a difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What might happen is an entirely different -- anything can happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You cannot hold up proceedings because something might happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No, but I am merely trying to demonstrate the potential relationship that exists between the on-going inquiry and this trial. They cannot be viewed completely in isolation, one from the other, there is a relationship. The defendant is a defendant in this trial and a potential defendant in another trial. It is a matter between the two things there is a relationship. They are not things which you pigeon hole and say they are completely separate and can have no effect one upon the other. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much, Mr. Greaves. I am directing this to the Prosecutor. How long do you think it will take you to make up your mind, because, as you very well would agree, there is a fundamental relationship between this case and the fall-out which is now affecting Delalic, because it all arose out of the same transaction which is the apparent case. If you really want to continue, definitely you put his mind at rest whether you are proceeding against him for the contempt of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: May I add before you answer, I think Mr. Delalic in his statement to the President has disowned the interview, that he did not give any interview at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. To make up our mind to do or not to do anything can be made very, very quickly. This is not up to me. I have to, of course, consult with the Prosecutor, Madam Arbour, about this. I believe that something should be done. The prosecution must take this invitation from the Honourable President earnestly and really make up their mind what to do or to decide we are not going to pursue this. The question whether we are going to pursue or not pursue I can bring to the Trial Chamber pretty quickly, I suppose, during this day even. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: This is exactly what I want to hear. We can get to know what you intend doing in view of the evidence before everyone here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The impression which I have gathered -- maybe my impression is incorrect -- the reporter or the journalist is not prepared to give any statement. This is my impression. I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You can have any guess -- it is a good guess what should happen. Something might be done. I can give you an answer to the question if we are going to pursue or if we are not going to pursue it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: As a rule the journalists never disclose the source of their information. They have gone to jail on so many occasions, but they do not give the source of their information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I am very well aware of that, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Is it possible we assemble here again at 4.30 to hear a decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Sorry, your Honour. I did not quite hear. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: If we can assemble today by any time this afternoon to hear a decision, because I think we are receiving Madeleine Albright here about 2 o'clock or 3 o'clock, I suppose. After that still about 4 o'clock we should be able to --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I will be back with some kind of an answer, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Let us know exactly what is going on instead of keeping us --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Of course. We have the same interest, of course. Our fundamental idea of what is going to go on is quite clear from what I have said before. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: For me personally it was a little difficult for counsel for Delalic to have the matter hanging over the head of him arising out of the same proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I appreciate their concerns. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: So we will rise and reassemble at about 4 o'clock. (11.10 am)

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: (4.00 pm) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Can we hear the reports from the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. We have tried to give copies of a written statement to the court and to the defence lawyers, and I will not read it out: I will just point to the main points in it, these points being that the prosecution looks upon the on-going trial and the contempt issue as two separate matters. In the submission of the prosecution there is no reason for delay and we can see no conflict of interests between defence lawyer and defendant. However, there is an obligation in the submission of the prosecution to pursue the contempt issue, and that is impossible for the prosecution to predict the outcome or the time-frame of such an investigation, and, lastly, that the prosecution cannot possibly promise not to bring charges that would grant some kind of immunity from contempt proceedings to anybody, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Before you sit down, a few clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I am sure you have relied on the reports of the President in respect of these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Now that is not a parallel future investigation, because you have made a complaint to the Trial Chamber and that complaint was referred for investigation and investigation has reported and in their report a recommendation was made for a possible prosecution. You exercise your discretion. Does that mean you have found there is not sufficient evidence for proceeding with the contempt proceeding relying on that -- on the facts of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: As far as the defence lawyers go. On the other hand there was an attempt to assist the prosecution whether it has to go on on its own to find out what is behind this very grave matter. That is what the Prosecutor has decided to do. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I am not challenging what you have decided to do. What I am saying is all your actions have impinged on the report of the investigation so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, so far. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is all I wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond to that, the prosecution made a complaint and produced before the Tribunal evidence, such as it is, of two articles written and the list of witnesses. This is not a question of hypothesis. Those documents exist; the list of witnesses exist. The whole of the procedure hitherto followed by the Honourable President was to attempt to investigate this matter based upon the complaint, the source of the complaint put before the Tribunal by the prosecution. It falls within a fairly narrow register. The principal person who, in my submission, could assist this Tribunal in the determination of the central issue and the central issue is in reality an allegation against Mr. Delalic of contempt is the named journalist in paragraph 6 of the President's report, Mr. Tahir Pervan and an unnamed editor. It seems to me, with the greatest respect, that the only evidence that would be capable of founding a charge of contempt would flow from information from Mr. Pervan and the editor. Those are the people who would have received the information. Those are the people who would have been responsible for its publication. So we are not dealing with long-term or impossible hypotheses. We are dealing with hard information that already exists, the two articles and named people who are the best possible source of the information that this Tribunal might want. If it was the case that the prosecution were saying that they had no present intention to investigate this matter until the conclusion of the proceedings, that would be one thing, and one would have to look at that upon its merits, but what the prosecution say in the second paragraph of their response is that they do not have evidence such that it may bring contempt charges and thus has no present intention to bring contempt charges against anyone. What it does not say is there is no present intention to investigate the matter until the conclusion of the case. Indeed, the first sentence of the third paragraph says in reality just the opposite: "The prosecution intends to vigorously pursue how names of particular witnesses were published and the possible violation of court orders". I take no point as to that. The prosecution have been invited by the learned President in the last paragraph of his report to consider whether it is appropriate to initiate proceedings. The only way whether they can see whether it is appropriate to initiate proceedings is to vigorously pursue the case to get the evidence, but that falls, in my submission, into a very small compass in this case. What is not going to assist this Tribunal, and I now go to the latter part of the third paragraph of the prosecution response to the inquiry, if in two days or in two years or, indeed, in two months or two weeks this matter is again brought to a standstill because of a desire to investigate or something else that is discovered that could be discovered by a relatively simple inquiry now. The reality of the position is this, that if Mr. Tahir Pervan and the editor of the newspaper in question are simply going to refuse to give evidence, it is impossible to see in as much as one can see into the future as a reasonable Prosecutor, a reasonable advocate, how there could be any evidence to bring in contempt before the court as a charge. It is a relatively easy matter to determine. It is not going to get any better if it is left in abeyance for two days, two weeks, two months or two years. This is an issue, as I said this morning, which goes to the very heart of the case. There was a suggestion made just a moment ago, with the greatest respect, that contempt and the trial are two separate issues. That is not the case in my respectful submission. If the contempt and the evidence were two separate issues, I doubt very much if the prosecution in this case would have raised the issue as and when they did or brought any suggestion that anyone in particular might have been responsible for the contempt. It is because that contempt goes to the very heart of the evidence that they raise the matter in the way they did. They are inseparable, interwoven, and they cannot easily be taken apart except by determination that the available evidence or available source of evidence is simply not sufficient. The visit of Madeline Albright, in my respectful submission, today, your Honour, is a useful demonstration how this Tribunal operates in the eyes of the world. It has a group of eminent and carefully selected judges, and the world community is, therefore, entitled to look at the Tribunal's decisions and to find the highest and most careful considerations being given to the fundamental issues and the rights of those being tried before this Tribunal. Similar exacting standards are, of course, expected of the prosecution and the defence both as entities and by individual professionals. Here we have a case where Mr. Delalic's counsel, Madame Residovic and Professor O'Sullivan, have plainly indicated that they cannot continue to represent Mr. Delalic on the main issue until the collateral issue of contempt is determined. I hark back to the very first words that your Honour spoke this morning. The object of the exercise of the last week or so has been to determine this issue. The danger is that we may not be a further step forward. Now, this is not an allegation, as I say, of a minor contempt. It is one which goes to the very core of the evidence and which has the most serious implications for the probity and weight of that evidence. Indeed, it is arguable that if it is proved, it is not merely a contempt, but it is either an attempt to pervert or an actual perversion of the course of justice, one of the most serious matters that comes before a criminal court. The argument that evidence can be properly received and judicially considered without the prior determination of an issue of that magnitude without glaring risk of prejudice to both the defence and, frankly, to the Prosecution is fundamentally flawed and raises, in my submission, avoidable difficulties. It is a rhetorical question, but justice would not be seen to be done by the world community in this case if an avoidable issue was not avoided. I propose, in my submission, the following simple steps. The basis for the collation of the evidence is plain. It is the individuals that I have named. With diligence that could be done in a matter of days. Its weight could be considered in a matter of hours within the competence of any experienced Prosecutor. They then make a final decision whether or not to prosecute. That really is done at one and the same time as the weight of the evidence is considered. It is based upon the quality of the evidence. If the decision is made not to prosecute, having considered that evidence, then all well and good. One can immediately restart the trial. If they do decide to prosecute, having considered any evidence from the two individuals from whom it is likely to come, that is disclosed as it is disclosable within the rules and as necessary for the defence to take necessary steps to seek and clarify it. That is a matter of days. With the greatest respect, if I was involved, a matter of a day or two. I see no difficulty or complication in that. The matter then comes before this Tribunal to try the contempt issue as rapidly as practicable. I would estimate a day or two. With expedition, this could and ought to be done in a timescale that need not exceed two weeks. It is relatively quick, it is simple and as far as the issue is concerned, has the enormous advantage and benefit of being final, because there would be a determination by the Tribunal on the evidence. That, in my respectful submission, is the proper judicial and jurisprudence course. Anything else is not only second best, but it is likely to create more difficulties and delays than it solves. I anticipate, with the greatest respect, that this Tribunal being of the nature and the seniority that it is, is not interested in second best. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Mr. Moran, you have something to add to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think you have caught it but in the outside chance that you did not see it, I will just point out two things. The second to the last paragraph in the Prosecutor's submission begins: "Presently there has been no evidence presented in the current proceeding suggesting that any accused has committed contempt". I would suggest that the Trial Chamber compares that with paragraph 7 (b) of President Cassese's report this morning. I would suggest one of two things has occurred. Either I have greater faith in President Cassese's ability as a fact-finder than other parties, but the prosecution does not consider the judicial inquiry to be the current proceeding. Clearly I think paragraph 7 (b) presents some evidence. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I am not sure the Prosecutor interpreted it the same way you do. He did not come to the same conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Like I say, it very well could be that they take a much narrower view of what President Cassese had found and than I do. I may take a broader view of his findings. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually we are not going into the merits of what the report looks like now. A recommendation has been made to the Prosecutor to do certain things and they have decided to do other things. He had in his own presentation indicated that he was not actually proceeding with the prosecution for contempt, but he is deciding to do other things outside that. That is quite different. Ms. Residovic? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, in addition to what has already been said by my learned colleagues, I should like to make a few additional remarks, namely it is correct that in paragraph 2 of this report the Prosecutor said that for the present he has no intention to prosecute, but also in the third paragraph he says that he intends to pursue another path that you, your Honour, have just referred to. Thereby the situation we found ourselves in at the beginning has not been substantively changed, because the last sentence of the third paragraph states clearly that the Prosecutor will pursue the investigation for two days or two years, and he also says that no one can be in advance relieved of any responsibility. I , therefore, see a certain contradiction between this position of the Prosecutor presented in his response and the position when he said that at this moment he does not see the evidence to be able to bring contempt charges and especially no evidence that defence counsel had any part in all this. The sentence that: "Noone, the accused or anyone else, can be exempted from this investigation by the Prosecutor", actually places ourselves in the same position that we found ourselves in at the beginning of the discussion of this case. The Prosecutor sees no conflict of interest and he elaborates on this. I should like to draw attention at the last paragraph of the prosecution's statement. I think there was a misunderstanding of the position taken by Mr. Delalic's defence counsel, namely if the position of his defence counsel in this case were completely clear and that there was absolutely no suspicion and that there was no evidence today or tomorrow against them, the question of their professional and ethical attitude towards the client remains open, and according to them they cannot participate in the proceedings if those proceedings are linked to the investigation the Prosecutor intends to conduct, and in the course of that investigation certain evidence may be presented which could be to the detriment of the defendant. Our distinguished colleague, Mr. Greaves, tried to give an example of such a possible situation. The Prosecutor offers a possibility which is in accordance with the rules of this Tribunal, namely it is true that colleague O'Sullivan and myself were appointed by this Tribunal as defence counsel. It is also true that this Tribunal has the possibility to appoint other defence counsel, which they feel would best protect his interests and ensure a fair trial. I cannot speak on behalf of future potential counsel, but I know that as an attorney, if I were to find myself in a situation to participate in a proceedings when, due to an investigation which may last two days or two years, and if this could result in any prejudice towards my defendant, I would not be able to participate in such proceedings. However, as I cannot speak on behalf of anybody else but myself, I just wish to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why not take paragraph 2 as it is and proceed further in the matter? In the event the prosecution gets any information that anybody is responsible for the leakage the prosecution will bring it to our notice and we will consider what is to be done. At this stage there is no evidence at all, merely on the assumption that something might be found we hold up the trial. I just do not understand that. Take the paragraph as it is. There is no evidence against anyone at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, I think it is probably for me to try to answer the inquiry which your Honour has made. It is this, that we are operating within a very small sphere here. It is not suggested that there is a large group of people who are potential contemnors. It is suggested that Mr. Delalic is a contemnor. It is suggested he has acted in concert with two named individuals. That is apparent from the article itself. If those two named individuals are seen by an independent investigator and unequivocally state that they have no intention of giving evidence or coming before this Tribunal, then I find it wholly inconceivable how this issue of contempt could be taken any further. That is resolvable in a very short space of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: May I say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The prosecution concedes that at this stage it has no evidence. Maybe from some other source apart from these press men later on, maybe after this trial is over, it comes to know who is responsible for the leak. Would it not give any finding -- if the prosecution gives any undertaking, would it not bind its hands in future?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: If the prosecution were to give an undertaking that they would not pursue this matter of contempt until the conclusion of the main indictment, I can see how that is a suggestion that would have to be carefully considered on its merits by the defendant, and I cannot speak without obviously consulting him, and would also, no doubt, be considered by other counsel who appear before him, but that is not what is said. What is said is it has no present intention to bring contempt charges. That is, with respect, not much of an offer. Without evidence they could not bring contempt charges. It is rather like me saying that I have no present intention of winning the 100 metres at the next Olympics. It is a matter of impossibility. I cannot do that. They are in exactly the same impossible situation. I undertake not to try to train to win the 100 metres at the next Olympics. If they undertake not to try to obtain any evidence until the conclusion of the trial, that is a different matter. It is a very small compass and it is resolvable within a very small compass. I am not seeking delay; I am seeking expedition. This matter can be resolved quickly by the efficient use of the procedures which are available. I see terrible difficulties ahead if it is simply left in abeyance that it might be resolved in two days, two weeks, two months or two years.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just briefly respond, I think your Honour has -- I think the prosecution has tried to be very clear and honest with everyone about exactly the present situation, which is that there is now no evidence against anyone and now no intention to bring charges. Of course, it is the prosecution's duty to investigate the matter and it will do so, and although the prosecution, with all due respect, appreciates defence counsel's advice as to how to proceed and how long it will take, that is really a matter for the prosecution. The issue before this Chamber at the present time is; is there anything about a yet possible future investigation and what will happen in the future -- does it interfere with this case? Your Honour, certainly with respect to any of the accused there is absolutely nothing about the investigation which would now cause any problem with this trial proceeding. Your Honours are going to decide the indictment against the accused based upon the evidence brought before you, witnesses, documents admitted into evidence and such other things, and that is -- there cannot be any realistic suggestion that your Honours will base your decision on anything else. That is the issue now: can the proceedings -- the indictment against the four accused proceed? There is nothing which would mean that the contempt proceedings which are hypothetically in the future, which would cause any problems with this. In fact, even the investigation -- my respectful colleague, Mr. Morrison, suggests the prosecution should undertake not to investigate. Your Honour, there is no reason that the investigation is going to interfere again with the pending proceedings and, in fact -- at least the people on this bench will not be pursuing the investigation. The issue is: can this proceeding go forward, and I believe that is an issue for the accused and his defence Ms. Residovic and Mr. O'Sullivan. The prosecution can now not give anyone immunity. What the defence is now asking the prosecution to do is say right now: "We promise all of you immunity." We cannot do that with respect to ourselves, with respect to anyone, and there is no reason to do that. The only issue that I believe is a conflict of interest issue, and the prosecution does not believe that there is any conflict of interest, because we do not believe there is any evidence or even suggestion that defence counsel was involved in this. As defence counsel has pointed out, it is not the prosecution's job to decide on conflict of interest. We do not see one. If defence counsel, Ms. Residovic, because I do not believe that this is an issue for Mr. Morrison, with all due respect -- it is an issue for Ms. Residovic and Mr. O'Sullivan -- if they believe there is a conflict of interest, the prosecution regrets it and disagrees with it, but if that is the case and they continue with that, then the only thing we can suggest and this court is obligated to pursue these matters expeditiously, is that new counsel be appointed. If new counsel were appointed, there would be no conflict of interest, because certainly new counsel -- it cannot even be imagined hypothetically that new counsel would have had anything to do with the past possible contempt, and then these proceedings could go forward. Again, I emphasise we do not believe there is a conflict of interest. There is absolutely no evidence and absolutely no suggestion from anyone on the prosecution bench that Ms. Residovic or Mr. O'Sullivan were involved in this, but we cannot give anybody immunity, and there is no necessity to give anyone immunity, because what this Chamber is deciding at the present time is the indictment against the four accused. There are no contempt proceedings on-going. All that is on-going right now is the indictment against the four accused, which your Honours will have to decide based upon the evidence brought in the trial proceedings and, your Honour, we respectfully suggest that that can go on immediately. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think I had better get -- let us have our bearing. All we are discussing now is the reports of the investigation of the President into the complaint made to this Trial Chamber. The investigation came out to clear the two defence counsel of any wrongdoing and suggest a possible contempt proceedings against their clients, the first accused. Now, you have also looked into the proceedings and you have found that there is not sufficient evidence to prosecute for that contempt. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: At the present time, your Honour, that is exactly correct right based on the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is the case that based on the investigation done by the President in the report, the prosecution does not believe at the present time there is sufficient evidence to bring forth contempt proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you talking about sufficient evidence or no evidence? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: No evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you talking of sufficient evidence or no evidence? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: No evidence at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the prosecution -- if you would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Because I find from your response you said no evidence. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is what you stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Because insufficient evidence probably might include innuendos also. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Now follow the sequence I am adopting. You have also not found any evidence on which you have to prosecute the first accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Correct. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes. Now I do not see the basis of any further proceedings against anybody two weeks, two years or any other time. I find it difficult to see the basis for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, if -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Especially those involved in this investigation. I am not saying that you might not find other persons somewhere else who might be involved, but not these persons who have been investigated.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the prosecution believes that the President has invited the prosecution to consider whether it is appropriate to initiate proceedings against Mr. Delalic for contempt of the Tribunal. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The prosecution is going to consider that. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: No, it has now stated: " ... does not now have evidence".

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct. The prosecution does not now, based on this report, that is correct. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes. So in any event if you are not investigating the issue, you are only looking for other sources, not the same sources declared here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the prosecution does not understand the President's order to be a clearing of, for instance, all of the accused, nor does it interpret the President's order to mean that the prosecution cannot undertake as part of its own duties an investigation. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The prosecution is always obliged to investigate anything that it wants to investigate. It can do that, but when an investigation has started, which has in any event been inconclusive, well, I do not know. It depends on how you look at it, but I do not think it is wise even as a Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I understand your Honour's point but I do not believe that the prosecution interprets the President's report to mean that no further investigation can take place with respect to, for instance, Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If at any time any evidence comes to your notice that anyone is involved, will you immediately bring it to the notice of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Absolutely, your Honour. How could we not? We think we have an obligation to try to find --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Then we can consider what is to be done. At this stage there is no evidence but if at any stage you get any evidence, will you immediately bring this to the notice of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the difficulty with this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There should be no difficulty, because if there is any evidence available involving anyone, they will bring it to our notice, and we can consider what will be done, whether the trial is to be held up so the whole thing is cleared up or nothing is to be done further. At this stage it is too premature to say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is an observation with which I , with respect, entirely agree. It is an observation which should have had its effect when this information first came into the hands of the prosecution. The prosecution chose, to use an English expression, to raise a hare. The hare is running --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: May I say something before you start? You have seen the second article, not the interview but the second article, that the list of witnesses is available to so many people. The defence counsel insist on the paper not to publish the list because it might affect their duty towards the Tribunal. So defence counsel were, in fact, against the publication of any list. How did the paper obtain the list? The paper has indicated -- the article itself indicates from where it could have obtained the list for a small amount of money. At the moment there is nothing against anyone, not only Delalic, because he has disowned the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the greatest of respect, exactly. If that had been the position without it being raised and left to this Tribunal and the defendants and the defence, in the last week or thereabouts, however long it has been and I can't say because I have not been here, this trial would have carried on hearing the evidence on indictment as if nothing has happened, because in reality nothing had happened up until the prosecution made it happen. The prosecution did not produce evidence. They produced supposition. With the greatest of respect, what should have happened is that the prosecution should have put into train an investigation to see if there was evidence, and that evidence should have been put before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Then they would have another complaint by the defence that "they are investigating us", so they brought it to our notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: That may be the case, but in my respectful submission, that would have been the proper way, the judicial with a small "j" way of doing it, so that the Tribunal was presented with evidence and not with supposition. What we have ended up with is a long delay and no doubt considerable expense based upon supposition, and what have we ended up with? Supposition. We are no further forward, but what it has created -- the only thing that has come out of it is ill. What it has created is this difficulty for the defendant Mr. Delalic and his counsel. To say there was not a suggestion he has been involved in contempt is disingenuous. There has plainly been a suggestion before the Tribunal that he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is why the prosecution have said plainly in paragraph 2 "we have no evidence." I am not using the word "insufficient" as used by Miss McHenry. "No evidence against anyone." The doubt earlier created, that should clear it now, and their undertaking to inform the Tribunal the moment they get any evidence against anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, if the prosecution want to run after the hare, catch it and put it back in the box, I would be happier than anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They seem to have done in this paragraph 2. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually what worries me is the indefinite nature of whatever investigation you intend to pursue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: This, your Honour, has to do with the impossibility to predict what will be the result of an investigation. I cannot see a Prosecutor at the Tribunal, this one or anywhere, who could sit down and find a contempt such as this one we have experienced and not look into it. We started with the -- to try to find a fast way, having the President or somebody named by him, as we asked for, to see if it was possible to find a leak rapidly. That ended up in a way inconclusively, without any conclusion, and an invitation to continue to look at it in a matter of this gravity. It is impossible for a Prosecutor, I believe, to say: "We will do that in three weeks, four weeks." We cannot tell that. We think it is an obligation of the Prosecutor here, as always, to see if we can find and stop this, and I find it utterly important, looking on our responsibilities we have against the witnesses we bring and the protections we give them, and I can find no -- listening to Mr. Morrison that we should have kept quiet and gone on, I cannot see this would have been a possibility. We brought a fact, namely the fact that our protected and other witnesses had been divulged in the paper in the former Yugoslavia. I would like to say we can do this in one week, no problem, and in Mr. Morrison's words, to make it final, but this is against nature. It cannot be done. It cannot be done. We do not know -- one day every Prosecutor has to close its case and send it to the archives, of course, but this is not the situation for the moment, and it is the standpoint of the Prosecutor that we have to look into it and say we cannot say when it is finished. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: No, but in this case is it not the involvement of Delalic that is worrying now?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: That is of course worrying. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is the only thing you are pursuing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No. No. No. What the prosecution has in mind is not something so narrow. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: What is the person before the Trial Chamber who needs to be cleared of any wrongdoing?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: If you actually intend to follow his case as vigorously as you put it, you can follow the case to conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I can indeed. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Knowing the participation in the whole business.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: As this case stands, as far as I can see Mr. Delalic belongs to the suspects. He stands out as giving -- the man who gave the interview, the man who gave the names of at least somebody, etc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But he has disowned it and the paper does not say the list of witnesses comes from him. It does not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The same thing is we can again -- I can at least not say to be honest that that is easy to find out. I do not think it is easy to find out but I think it lies in the ambit of what the Prosecutor should do. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: No. Here is a person restricted somewhere. His mobility and his sources are controlled. You think you cannot try to check those things and know how easily he could be involved in the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Of course. It sounds to me an impossibility that this can be done in so much days and then we have exhausted our ways to find out what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There have been so many instances of fake interviews appearing in so many cases. Why not accept Mr. Delalic's statement as it is, unless you have evidence, and you have undertaken to bring any evidence that you have as soon as you receive it before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The standpoint of the Prosecutor is that we cannot promise a time frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is what I pointed out to Mr. Morrison. Maybe you get the evidence three or four years later. So how can you sort of bind yourself to any undertaking given at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: There is a time limit to everything, of course. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually has anyone contradicted his denial?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Not so far. This investigation has not even started. The investigation initiated by the invitation of the President has not yet started. It will not be pursued by any of us standing here. It will be some other organ of the Office of the Prosecutor. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It will be safer for you to announce how soon you can proceed with your investigation so that all those involved in this trial will know exactly how to take their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I have no mandate to say that to the Trial Chamber today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I would not want to repeat myself, your Honour, but the reality is that this does exist within a small compass. The learned President has found out the name of the journalist and his editor. With the greatest respect, it seems inconceivable that if evidence is not forthcoming from one or both of those two named individuals, then there will be no evidence forthcoming upon which any reasonable Tribunal could convict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: At this stage. At this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: At this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe some time later, maybe a month later they get the information from some other source. How can anybody bind themselves down at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, I am perhaps being misunderstood. I am not asking for immunity. I am not asking for a binding. What I am asking is that the investigation is carried out swiftly within the parameters of what is known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: And in reality that can be done quickly. There are two named individuals. With all the facilities at the disposal of the prosecution it is inconceivable, in my respectful submission, that they cannot be seen and this be determined. Is there anything that they are going to say that could remotely be considered as probative evidence in this case? Are they going to say anything? Are they going to be cautioned and simply keep quiet? That is something that an investigating detective has to do day in, day out in cases large and small. When he has done it, it usually takes an hour or two of careful questioning to determine what the outcome is. If that course is undertaken with these two people and they, as I anticipate, either stand upon their right of silence or simply refuse to give any indication at all, then the prospect of any evidence being gleaned from those sources, which are the principal and probably the only sources that the prosecution could rely upon, means that this matter can be made final. They can -- a line can be drawn underneath this element of the case. The Tribunal can get on with it. With the greatest respect to my learned friend, I do not see how this can take more than a few days if it is done with expedition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But you have seen the reply of the counsel who spoke to the President. He has advised his clients not to answer, to give any answers. Now, in my country journalists prefer to go to jail for contempt rather than disclose their source of information and I think this probably is the stance taken by the journalist in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: With great respect, your Honour, I suspect it will be. If he is seen by an empowered Prosecutor who interviews him under caution and he says that, then we can draw a line under this case, and that can be done very quickly indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But, as I said, maybe from some other source they find out who had disclosed the names, then would that not bind the hands of the prosecution at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: No. With respect, it would not. If the prosecution finds at some point in the future other evidence which goes to show that Mr. Delalic or anybody else is guilty of a contempt, of course they are free to consider that information, and if it is viable, bring it before the Tribunal, but that is speculative and in the future. This is not speculative. These are names that are known. These are articles which have been written and are known. Their parameters and their contents are finite. There is nothing in this for speculation. This can be done very quickly indeed. Unless it is done, my fear is that this Tribunal is going to be put to a great deal more delay and expense than is necessary. This is a resolvable problem. What it needs is someone, with the greatest respect, to -- I use another English expression, get a grip on it, get it over and done with in the Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will just briefly respond. With all due respect, it is not for defence counsel to tell the prosecution exactly how to conduct the investigation or how long it will take. The prosecution will undertake vigorously an investigation and, as the Chamber has directed, we will immediately notify the Chamber if there is evidence against anyone involved, but at the present time there are no contempt proceedings.
