If there are later hypothetical contempt proceedings, they do not and need not affect these proceedings, and the prosecution believes that we can go forward immediately with this trial. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have tried quite hard to remain silent throughout this, and I find it now impossible. I rise with the indulgence of the court more in the nature of amicus curiae. It seems to me that a great lot is being made out of very little with regard to this matter. The prosecution has now had 13 days since they discovered this. On the first day this was discovered the name of the journalist who wrote the article was known to the Prosecution. I do not know how many investigators are employed by the Prosecutor's office, but it is a lot. There are several of them. It seems to me that it is so simple to put an investigator on an airplane, send him to see this journalist and find out if the journalist is going to talk. I think that quickly deals with the issues that are before this court. I am getting very frustrated with the delays that are being caused in this case by what I think is a matter that could have been solved rather quickly and can still be solved rather quickly. This court, I believe, contrary to what the prosecution has suggested to you, based upon its responsibility to the defendants in case and to justice, has certain supervisory powers over the conduct of the prosecution and over the conduct of the defence, and I think it would be entirely appropriate for this court to order the prosecution within the next three days to have an investigator contact these two witnesses that have been identified by President Cassese and report back as to whether or not they are willing to give statements regarding this matter. If they are not, I think that ends it. If they are, then we will have information. My guess is they are going to say: "We're not talking to anybody", and that we can move forward with this trial. We should be able to do that as quickly as Monday or Tuesday. If I were to stand up in this court at the end of the defence case and say to your Honours, as the Prosecutor is saying to you now: "I have learned information in the course of listening to the Prosecution's case that requires me to conduct an investigation. I have no idea how long that will take your Honours. I will let you know when the defence is ready to put on the defence case", you would find that outrageous. You would not permit me to do that. Yet the prosecution stands up in this court and says: "But we are the prosecution and we are permitted to take as long as we want to conduct an investigation and cause as many difficulties to this case as we want, because we are the prosecution." I think it is totally appropriate for this court to say: "No. You are ordered to conduct what investigation you want to conduct especially with regard to this reporter and this editor by Monday and tell us by Monday whether you have found out any information or not. If they are not going to talk to you, then we are going forward Monday afternoon or Tuesday morning, or whenever, but we need to move this case". Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much, Mr. Ackerman. If you look at paragraph 6 of the President's report, the unwillingness of Tahir Pervan to give evidence there before a magistrate or by telephone has been very clearly stated. He has no intention to give any evidence. In addition to that when, in fact, the President got back to his counsel, his counsel clearly stated he has advised the editor or Pervan not to say anything. Now, I do not know what going there again would do to such a group of persons. I suppose the presence of an investigator there might make a difference, but it seems fairly clear that they are not cooperating, and if this is the only source of evidence against the suspect, I think it is fairly remote to think that one can get anything other than being fanciful or guessing as to what had transpired between them. It appears the prosecution is taking a different line of action. What they are now doing possibly is to investigate a different line, not actually the terms of reference which talks about the leakage of the information to the press, but whether Delalic was the one who disclosed certain names to the journalists. This is -- I do not know whether -- this is not in my opinion from the terms of reference. The terms of reference were quite clear and precise. I agree it is contempt if the first accused did that, but whether that is part of the whole proceedings is a different matter. At any stage the prosecution is entitled to investigate whatever has been an offence within the Tribunal and they are free to do that, but whether it falls within the parameters of the reference is what really beats me. Since they are bent on investigating it, I suppose they will have to do the investigation and report to the Trial Chamber, but, you see, if from their first -- second paragraph here, if they have no evidence now for contempt proceedings, it means the investigation is looking for evidence to support contempt proceedings. This is what occurs to me. (Pause).. We have some problems about the decision as relatively as easy as it is. I think a few difficulties still arise. Actually our problem is the unwillingness of counsel for Delalic to continue in the face of investigation. I do not know whether Ms. Residovic would not mind carrying on until it is solved, because there is no suspicion against you or Professor O'Sullivan. You have been cleared. The only subject matter for investigation the prosecution now says is your client. So I do not see how you are indicted or seriously affected by what is going on, because even if you want to withdraw, we are not sure what Delalic's position will be because he might object. Can we hear your views on what position you are taking on this matter? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Please allow me a moment to consult with my colleague. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that consultation is taking place, may I simply indicate paragraph 6 of the learned President's report. Though he deals with the position of Mr. Tahir Pervan, there is no indication that the editor has been seen or that his views have been determined. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, after consulting with my colleague Professor O'Sullivan, essentially we think that our professional and ethical position remains unchanged with respect to the former position. However, we have not consulted with our client, and our position being as it is, perhaps a consultation with our client would either re-confirm this position or provide additional explanations. However, our original position remains unchanged. Unfortunately Mr. Delalic is not here, so that we can re-confirm this position with him as well. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually is it your position that if your client is charged with contempt, you will be in a difficulty to defend him? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, we had not addressed that issue. We addressed the issue on the situation in which we would find ourselves when we would continue to represent our client during the course of the investigation that may point to a conflict of interest or a situation which would make the position of our client more difficult and in which we participate as his defence counsel. So that is the issue, not the right of the Prosecutor to conduct an investigation, or if he has any evidence to point to the person or persons responsible for the orders issued by the Tribunal. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The issue in this case now is the possibility of investigating your client for a possible contempt proceedings. That is the only thing that is in issue now. The prosecution says for the time being the investigation of the President has not revealed any evidence, but they keep their options open in case there is evidence. So it is only in that case that there will be a proceeding against him. Now, is it your suggestion that if such a situation arises, that is in conflict with your professional duty?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In any case, the prosecution bring to our notice any time they discover any evidence against your client. Why not defer your decision? If there is any evidence which is brought to our notice, we will immediately consider all the grounds which you are taking now. It is premature at the moment to take a final decision in this regard for you. There is no evidence so far. If there is any, it will be brought to your notice immediately. Then you can decide whether you want to continue or not. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You have a continuing duty to defend him whatever charges are brought against him, and that does not conflict with your position as defence counsel. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Madame Residovic, it is clear for the Trial Chamber, if you allow me, that with regard to defence counsel, Edina Residovic and Eugene O'Sullivan, there is no evidence of misconduct on their part according to the report of President Cassese and according to the report of the prosecution also, because they stated clearly: "The Prosecution has no evidence that any defence counsel was involved in any contempt, and the prosecution has not and does not suggest in any way that any defence counsel was involved". So for the trial chamber it is clear that both of you have not any problem to continue with the proceedings. So the only problem we have here is to determine the situation of Mr. Delalic according to the President's report but not against you and Professor O'Sullivan. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Yes. So we are revisiting the previous issue, and that is the issue of us as counsel when we asked to make sure there was no conflict and interest so that we could vigorously and could vigorously defend our client, which would constitute a fair and just trial before this Trial Chamber. This was our original position, and it is possible that it may have been resolved by some of the quotes you have just offered from the report of the President as well as the prosecution's response. However, with the continuing investigation, I do not see -- I cannot foresee how much conflict of interest can arise from it, and therefore, your Honours, I thought that at the beginning of this hearing today it seemed to me pretty clear that the prosecution had within a certain deadline to provide a clear answer whether there is any suspicion with respect to either of us so that we could continue with this trial, but in a continuing investigation it is always possible that this situation be brought back to its very beginning. I do not know whether I have been clear enough, but the continuing investigation against our client which can put him in a position like that continues to be a problem. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I do not see how you will abandon your client merely because there is proceedings against him for contempt, or there is a likelihood to be one. Nobody has said there is any now. There is nobody saying there is proceedings now. All the prosecution is saying is it is investigating whether there could be. So you do not abandon him by talking about your conflict, because I do not see what conflict. In fact, you are duty-bound to defend him as his counsel. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, at no time did we say before this Tribunal that we would leave the defence of our client. It was something that came from the other side of the bench. At this point we will continue to defend our client. We will continue to defend him before this Trial Chamber with no restrictions, provided there is no conflict of interest. We will continue to defend him and we will continue to respect his position. That issue was never raised among us. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. So you are not abandoning him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: We will just clarify. The prosecution does not believe there is any suspicion either against counsel. So the record is clear, I notice that Ms. Residovic has indicated that her client is not present. We note that three of the accused are not present. So the record is clear, I understand that all of the accused have waived their right to appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: To clarify the record on that point, I have conferred with my client. He has authorised me to waive his presence here this afternoon on his behalf for this hearing. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have been desperately trying not to say a word all afternoon on the grounds that occasional silence from Mr.. Greaves is probably a good thing. Can I offer this. I support my learned friend Mr.. Ackerman's suggestion. Those of us who have the responsibility from time to time of prosecuting cases at home have it as part of our task that we advise the Crown Prosecution Service as to what evidence should be sought. So I hope the Tribunal will accept from me that both my learned friend Mr.. Morrison and I , and I am sure other prosecutors in court have experience of directing what should be done in order to efficaciously bring a matter to fruition. I have been sitting here all afternoon trying to think of who in the next couple of years might possibly turn up out of the woodwork and proffer evidence to assist the prosecution in any way at all. There are a very limited number of places where I, if I was giving an advice on evidence in this case, could conceivably think of sending my investigators to go and ask questions. They are these: counsel for the defence could properly be interviewed. It is likely that they would say nothing, exercising their right of silence. The defendant can be interviewed. Again it is likely he would either exercise his right to silence or say a very limited amount of things. There are two other potential witnesses. One of those has already been seen. One of the reasons that he gives for being unable to travel to The Hague is he has lost his passport. There are ways round that. Travel papers can be provided to assist him to come to The Hague and give his account about it. There is one other person who comes to mind who might have information and that is the editor, who has not yet been seen. It will be the matter of a moment over this weekend for the Prosecutor's investigators to lay hands on this man and talk to him. As I say, beyond those people, I am struggling to think of anybody who is conceivably able to give any evidence relating to this matter. If I have missed somebody, I am sure the prosecution will no doubt bring that person's attention -- name to our attention. So the reality is, as my learned friend Mr.. Ackerman said, if your Honours are prepared to do this, you are entitled to direct the prosecution to conduct an investigation and to put a time limit on it, and to tell them: "If you have not come up with anything at that stage, that is an end of the matter." It will resolve every problem. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Mr.. Ostberg, have you any reaction to this before we terminate this dialogue?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I will indeed. We have heard suggestions as to what the Prosecutor should do to easily and rapidly conclude his investigation and come up with a final decision, and I have tried to bring to the Trial Chamber my view on that. That is not possible. That is not possible to do. There are lots of avenues that I am not mandated to bring to the Trial Chamber or the defence for the prosecution's investigating personnel to look into this matter. Of course, I cannot preclude the Trial Chamber to prevent the Prosecutor to do things and set up time-frames, but from the side of the prosecution I cannot promise to do just these few things that have been suggested. There are many other things to be done. I concur totally with your Honour in saying that this is, as far as I understood, nothing that prevents this trial to go on. We stand by our first view on this. These are two different matters and I do hope that Madam Residovic's sees no conflict of interest and that this trial can just go on, which is exactly what the prosecution wants to do. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually the position you are taking is that the investigation about the complicity of Delalic goes beyond the persons we have now known that are involved in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: It must also be encompassed in it. He is not ruled out and other persons who may pop up I can have no prediction of. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: So you still keep your likelihood of investigation to two weeks or two months or years, indefinite?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Might be. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Indefinite.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I have tried to say from my prosecutorial experience it is not possible to say this day and then it is final. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I understand you to say that he is still the subject matter of investigation for this purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. That is the position. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is what you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: That is the position. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: (Pause). I am very grateful for all the assistance counsel have given to the Trial Chamber in resolving this issue. I started with all optimism and good wishes. I thought that things were easy. I did not expect such a protracted argument for matters which are as simple as these are. The Prosecutor has decided that all is not over and that there is still something left for investigations. I suppose that is his discretion, if he wants to do it that way. I think the issues are not as simple as that. He knows the implications of delaying and those are difficulties that might ensue if things go contrary to how the arguments have been going and I think he will expedite every facility he has to make sure that this thing is concluded within a very short time. Now, I do not think counsel for Delalic will have any conflict. They have been very clear -- they have been cleared of any wrongdoing. If, in fact, it arises, all they need do here is to defend their client with all the vigour at their disposal, but I think also it is not in the best interests of the Prosecutor to delay clearing this fog which is still hanging around the accused persons. Even if one might say it is a little different from the same thing, it is still a matter which arises from the same transaction. The whole episode arose from the trial he is standing, and if there should be something incriminating against him in addition to his trial, it should be cleared as early as possible. It should not be allowed to hang over him and let him continue feeling jittery about its coming after. It is not unusual -- I am surprised that Mr.. Ostberg and Ms. McHenry are not comfortable with defence counsel making suggestions. I think it is a very common thing. It is common for defence counsel assisting suggesting as to how you can go about a particular Prosecution, because it is possible you have not thought about that. Some others with considerable experience might have adverted to this issue and found ways of getting over them. In this regard I still believe -- I agree with them -- the earlier the matter is settled, the better for everyone, because it does not reflect well on the prosecution, which had all the opportunities to turn over evidence to the President when he was making his investigation. You had all opportunity to make suggestions and direct us to what should be done when the investigation was going on. For the time being the Trial Chamber will adjourn until 10.00 am tomorrow. Thank you very much. (5.30 pm)
